FACULTY SENATE OFFICE 224 PASTORE HALL, 51 LOWER COLLEGE ROAD, KINGSTON, RI 02881 USA, P: 401.874.2616 Faculty Senate Resolution 2024-2025-03 Faculty Senate Meeting of January 23, 2025 Resolution on the Implementation of Honors Contracts WHEREAS, following considerable self-study and significant input from external experts, the URI Honors Program has proposed the use of honors contracts at URI.
Honors contracts are formal agreements, facilitated by an honors program, between a student and instructor.
They allow students and instructors to enhance non-honors courses to an honors level through additional learner-directed work tailored to the “broader, deeper, and more complex” learning experiences advocated by the National Collegiate Honors Council (NCHC); and WHEREAS, contracts are recognized by over 60% of honors programs in the USA, where they foster community and ownership by enhancing the educational process and commitment to the programs’ success.
For example, work at the University Honors Program at the University of Kansas shows that honors contracts act as far more than stopgaps to address honors course shortages.

They can “facilitate access to honors, increases completion, democratize key aspects of the honors experience, provide students with structured avenues for building relationships with faculty members, and empower students to own their educational experiences”; and WHEREAS, honors contracts may be best understood as a form of an independent study, entered into voluntarily by both students and faculty, with a contract defining outcomes, deadlines, and assessment definitions for additional work related to the course materials; and WHEREAS, honors contracts provide flexibility for students to align their education with their interests and goals.
They also allow programs to meet student needs when student/faculty constraints or funding limitations preclude offering stand-alone honors courses that fit student interests and needs; and WHEREAS, Contracts provide an extra measure of curricular flexibility at institutions such as ours that are not able to field enough faculty, cannot provide an adequate number of honors courses, or do not have a large enough student body to fill honors sections.

Contracts can fill the gap and provide opportunities for the self-guided intellectual growth of students; NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Faculty Senate of the University of Rhode Island calls for implementation of the following Honors Contracts Proposal.
This includes making the

recommended changes to the University Catalog and to the eCampus system used by Enrollment Services; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Honors Program is called upon to reflect these changes on their website and in all other promotional and outreach materials promulgated by the Program. The Program is also called upon to review Chapter 8 of the University Manual (Academic Regulations, Honors Program) in light of the Contracts Proposal and bring any recommended changes to the Faculty Senate expeditiously; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the authority to offer Honors Contracts enabled by this resolution shall not extend beyond the Fall 2025 semester; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that no instructor may participate in more than three Honors Contracts in a single semester. Adopted this 23rd day of January, 2025. ____________________________________________________________ T heodore Walls, URI Faculty Senate President

To stand out in a crowded market, programs often seek accreditation from prestigious bodies like AACSB, AMBA, or EQUIS and aim to secure favorable rankings from notable publications.
Many programs also forge partnerships with businesses and other organizations to help in curriculum development, provide real-world learning opportunities, and facilitate networking and job placements for graduates.

Recent trends in MSM programs include an increased emphasis on technology and analytics to integrate digital technologies in business, a focus on sustainability and social responsibility reflecting broader societal concerns, and more customizable and flexible learning paths to attract a diverse student body with varying needs and career goals.
Overall, the market for MSM programs remains robust, driven by their relevance, accessibility, and adaptability to market needs and educational technologies, though programs must continuously innovate and adapt to remain competitive.

Enrollment Management update - Associate Vice President Libutti presented hisreport on enrollment for Fall, 2023 which had been made available in advance.
Henoted his data came from the Office for Institutional Research and he encouragedfaculty to visit that website for more detailed data and useful data visualizationtools.
Highlights of the report included the success the university is having atpreventing “summer melt,” a number that has been cut nearly in half.
The universityalso continues to grow its Talent Development program numbers and its percentageof “first in family” enrollees.
Also, for the first time, URI enrolled more out of statestudents than in-state students, which was not by design.
A couple of concerns formoving forward were noted.
First, there is a need for more student housing both oncampus and within the broader community.
It is especially concerning thatneighboring towns are increasingly hostile toward student rentals.
The universityhas had to reintroduce triple rooms which was not met with enthusiasm.
Promisingstudents, including graduate students, could be lost to competing universitiesbecause of housing.

Second, competing universities in other states are out-pacingURI in terms of ABM programs and in terms of regionalized tuition discounts(attending for an in-state rate).
This could harm enrollment in the future.
Third,there are concerns about the limitations of the Hope and Promise Scholarships andthe need for URI to be included in the state’s programs.
Other states are expandingsimilar programs, which stands to negatively affect Rhode Island, but moreimportantly, there is a question of equity and fairness for students who deserveaccess to all educational options.
Other topics were also discussed, like enrollmentby college, student preparedness, modality preferences, and overall well-being,along with the percent of adult learners/Finish What You Started programparticipants.

TheCommittee has examined active RFA’s at peer institutions to develop a formalproposal for such organization here.
An Association would be expected to play a rolein advocacy (for various benefits and access in retirement) and in providingopportunities for connection, community and social contact.
The Committee isconsidering developing a Handbook for retired faculty that would provideinformation on issues of common interest and certain privileges that should beextended to retired faculty.
Currently, there seems to be a lot of uncertainty aroundwhich retired faculty members are extended Emeritus status and what ongoingprivileges extend to retirees (like IT support, parking, library use, attendance atathletic, cultural and other events, etc.).

Clark stressed the mutual benefits of anRFA, noting retired faculty are a reservoir of experience and wisdom that couldcontinue to serve the community.

Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-2
November 14, 2024 Faculty Senate Meeting
Context (from JCODL 2022-2023 final report): “Several years ago (circa 2013), URI adopted definitions of online and blended learning (Face to face [< 25% online], Blended [25-75% online], and Online [75-100% online]), with the implicit, but unstated, assumption that the online portion was asynchronous. The COVID era of remote instruction gave rise to additional approaches to remote instruction and the need to reflect all available modality options and to provide clear, comprehensible and accessible definitions and descriptions for the benefit of faculty and students.”
Existing Language:
https://web.uri.edu/registration-records/faculty-staff-advisors/class-scheduling-process/.
“In-person (I): A course with no more than 24.9% of instruction delivered online. All courses are assumed to be in-person unless otherwise approved by Faculty Senate.
Blended (B): A course delivered 25%-74.9% online.
Online (O): A course delivered at least 75% online. Course must be approved as online by Faculty Senate to be scheduled as such.”
Proposed Language:

(To be inserted into Chapter 8 of the University Manual, “Academic Regulations.”)
“8.30.30 Course Modality
In-person: All instruction occurs in a specified physical location and on specified days/times.
In-person and online asynchronous: Instruction combines both in-person meetings on specified days/times and online asynchronous instruction. The schedule of instruction and the weekly time commitment to online asynchronous instruction are clear to students in the syllabus on the first day of class.
Online synchronous: All instruction occurs online at specified days/times.
Online synchronous and asynchronous: All instruction occurs online in a combination of synchronous meetings on specified days/times and asynchronous instruction. The schedule of instruction and the weekly time commitment to online asynchronous instruction are clear to students in the syllabus.
Online asynchronous: All instruction occurs online with no synchronous meetings required at specified days/times (outside of optional online office hours/meetings). The weekly time commitment to online asynchronous instruction is clear to students in the syllabus.”
Clean Version:
“8.30.30 Course Modality

In-person: All instruction occurs in a specified physical location and on specified days/times.
In-person and online asynchronous: Instruction combines both in-person meetings on specified days/times and online asynchronous instruction. The schedule of instruction and the weekly time commitment to online asynchronous instruction are clear to students in the syllabus on the first day of class.
Online synchronous: All instruction occurs online at specified days/times.
Online synchronous and asynchronous: All instruction occurs online in a combination of synchronous meetings on specified days/times and asynchronous instruction. The schedule of instruction and the weekly time commitment to online asynchronous instruction are clear to students in the syllabus.
Online asynchronous: All instruction occurs online with no synchronous meetings required at specified days/times (outside of optional online office hours/meetings). The weekly time commitment to online asynchronous instruction is clear to students in the syllabus.”

“Lecture: A course in which the primary method is presentation and students are expected to participate in a variety of ways, such as small-group discussions, questions and answers, writing-exercises, etc.

Laboratory: In-class applied course work, generally involving experimentation or observation, typically using special equipment (including computers and specialized software).
Recitation: Separate sections of a lecture course regularly scheduled for discussion.
Studio: In-class, supervised work with an emphasis on performance and creativity in which faculty instruct, assist, and critique.
Seminar: Course offered to a small group (usually no more than 20 students) where participants actively exchange ideas and findings based on readings or research.
Independent Study: One-on-one instruction in which the student enters into an agreement with the instructor that defines the focus of inquiry and nature of activities. Includes tutorials, directed readings, special projects.
Practicum: Structured experiences where the primary aim is to connect theory with practice. Includes clinics, internships, externships, student teaching, field experiences. May include regular class meetings.
Workshop: Similar to a seminar, with emphasis on applied rather than theoretical learning, but not offered for degree-program credit.

Online: A course that is delivered entirely online. (CAC policy includes possibility of a required organizational session, etc.)”
